conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: TrianglePattern
candidates.quote: The minimum requirement for a trading range to be called a triangle is that it has three pushes up or down... All triangles have at least three legs in one direction and at least two in the other.
candidates.description: Shared primitive for this chapter: a triangle is any trading range with at least three swing pushes in one direction and at least two in the other, contained between two lines (a horizontal/trend-line boundary on each side). Ascending, descending, symmetrical, contracting, and expanding triangles are all this same structure; a sloped version with tight, converging lines is a wedge (R18-01).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (pattern classification used as a signal precondition)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and a push counter over a variable-length window; distinguishing subtypes (expanding/contracting/ascending/descending) needs the two boundary lines' slopes as well

notes: Brooks treats 'more than five pushes' as just relabeled a trading range with no behavioral difference; not modeled as a separate threshold.
Every trading-range measured-move / final-flag / near-extreme-fade primitive already defined elsewhere in this book can compose with this pattern.

candidates.name: OutsideOutsideExpandingTrianglePattern
candidates.quote: An oo (outside-outside) pattern, where an outside bar is followed by a larger outside bar, is a small expanding triangle.
candidates.description: Two-bar primitive: an outside bar (engulfs the bar before it) is immediately followed by an even larger outside bar (engulfs the first outside bar) -- a miniature expanding triangle.

complexity.reason: a two-bar chained outside-bar comparison, no pivot detection needed

notes: Similar in spirit to the catalog's Harris multi-bar patterns (fixed-offset comparisons), but not a duplicate of any of them.

candidates.name: TriangleHeightMeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: If it breaks out in either direction, the breakout usually leads to a measured move approximately equal in points to the height of the channel.
candidates.description: After a triangle breakout, project a measured-move profit target equal to the triangle's height (its upper extreme to its lower extreme) added from the breakout point.
candidates.book_order_type: limit exit (or discretionary scale-out) at the measured-move price

complexity.reason: the extremes require the same swing-pivot detection as R23-01; the projection arithmetic itself is trivial

notes: Same measured-move family as R18-08, R20-07, and TradingRangeHeightTarget (chapter 8); likely mergeable into one generic pattern-height measured-move exit.

candidates.name: TriangleBreakoutBeyondTargetSignalsTrendContinuationFilter
candidates.quote: If it goes beyond that, the market is likely in a trend.
candidates.description: Once price extends beyond the triangle's measured-move target (R23-03) rather than stalling there, treat the market as likely transitioning into a trend: favor with-breakout continuation entries over range-style fades of the target level.
candidates.pseudocode:
beyondMeasuredMove = close[0] > measuredMoveTarget; // long breakout case
likelyEnteringTrend = beyondMeasuredMove;

complexity.reason: a single comparison once the measured-move target (R23-03, itself hard) already exists

candidates.name: FadeTriangleExtremesWhenTallEnoughFilter
candidates.quote: when the pattern is tall enough, you can trade it like a trading range and fade the extremes, looking to buy near the bottom and sell near the top.
candidates.description: Only permit fading a triangle's extremes (buying near its bottom, selling near its top) when the triangle's height is large enough relative to recent volatility to leave room for a worthwhile scalp; otherwise treat it like a tight trading range and stand aside (see chapter 22).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (entry permission gate); fade entries themselves as in R21-03..R21-10

complexity.reason: inherits R23-01's swing-pivot detection for the triangle extremes, plus an ATR-based height-sufficiency test and the range-location filter

notes: Complements R22-01 (TightTradingRangeWidthTest): a triangle failing the 'tall enough' test here is effectively a tight trading range and should instead be governed by R22-04 (block all entries).

candidates.name: TriangleWithTrendBreakoutBiasFilter
candidates.quote: A triangle in a bull trend usually breaks out to the upside, and a bear triangle usually breaks out to the downside... They tend to break out slightly more often in the direction of the trend that preceded them, but not enough to place a trade on that basis alone.
candidates.description: A weak bias filter: within a triangle, mildly prefer breakout entries in the direction of the prior always-in trend. Recorded as stated even though Brooks says the edge alone is too small to trade on.

complexity.reason: reuses the existing AlwaysInDirection primitive; the bias itself is a single comparison

notes: Brooks explicitly says this bias is 'not enough to place a trade on that basis alone'; kept for recall as a weighting input, not a standalone entry signal.
Same family as R22-07 (PreferWithTrendBreakoutAfterTightRangeFilter, chapter 22) applied to triangles specifically.

candidates.name: WedgeBreakoutRequiresStrengthConfirmationFilter
candidates.quote: traders should not buy the first reversal up or the bull breakout of the wedge. They should wait until the bull breakout occurs and then evaluate its strength. If the breakout is strong... they should wait for a pullback and then enter at the end of the pullback (a breakout pullback buy). If there is no pullback for several bars, then the market is forming a strong bull spike and has almost certainly become always-in long.
candidates.description: When uncertain whether a steep wedge will reverse, do not enter on the wedge's breakout bar itself. Wait to classify the breakout's strength (chapter 2's strong-breakout characteristics); if strong, enter on the breakout pullback, or -- if no pullback forms for several bars -- trade the resulting spike directly as an always-in-long continuation.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop on the breakout pullback signal bar, or buy at market/close during a strong no-pullback spike

complexity.reason: needs a breakout-strength classifier (chapter 2) plus the wedge/triangle pattern and the breakout-pullback primitive

notes: This is the chapter's practical trading procedure for wedges of uncertain reliability; sits alongside R18-01/R21-05 (buying a wedge bull flag) as the more cautious variant.

candidates.name: DownWedgeAlwaysActsAsBullFlagFilter
candidates.quote: Any down wedge will behave like a large pullback in a bull trend, which means that it will behave like a bull flag... every bear channel, whether or not the lines converge and create a wedge, functions like a bull flag and should be thought of as a bull flag.
candidates.description: Treat any down-sloping wedge or bear channel as a bull-flag context and favor an eventual upside breakout, even when the visible chart shows an established bear trend leading into it (mirrored: an up-sloping wedge/bull channel is always a bear flag).

complexity.reason: requires a design decision: this context claim is meant to override whatever larger-trend detector the engine otherwise uses, which needs care to implement without creating a rule that always fires the same way

notes: Brooks's most counterintuitive claim in the chapter: even a wedge that 'fills the entire screen' in an apparent bear trend should be read as a bull flag.

candidates.name: ExpandingTriangleAlternatingReversalContinuationFilter
candidates.quote: Once they break out, the breakout often fails and the market then reverses, breaks out of the other side, and forms an even larger expanding triangle. The expanding triangle reversal then becomes a continuation pattern, and an expanding triangle continuation pattern then becomes a reversal.
candidates.description: Expanding triangles tend to alternate role: a breakout failure from one expanding triangle typically forms a larger expanding triangle on the opposite side, flipping whether the pattern is best read as a reversal or a continuation.

complexity.reason: needs a way to detect a failed expanding-triangle breakout and a nested, growing expanding-triangle structure -- no bar-level test is given

candidates.name: TriangleLateInTrendFinalFlagFilter
candidates.quote: Because they are more complex than one-push pullbacks (high 1 and low 1 pullbacks) and two-push pullbacks (high 2 and low 2 pullbacks), they represent stronger countertrend pressure. Since traders in the opposite direction are getting stronger, these patterns tend to occur late in trends and swings, and often become final flags.
candidates.description: A triangle forming after a trend has already run for a while is likely to be the trend's final flag (the last pullback before the trend ends), because a three-push pullback signals stronger countertrend pressure than a one- or two-push pullback.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context classification feeding an exit or reversal-entry decision defined elsewhere)

complexity.reason: composes the triangle primitive with a bars-since-trend-start counter; 'late in the trend' is a reading, not a stated threshold

rejected.quote: The daily chart of Intel (INTC) presented in Figure 23.2 had many triangles, which are rarely ever perfect.
rejected.reason: acknowledges that fitting a triangle's boundary lines to real charts is a subjective drawing exercise with no numeric criterion given here beyond the push-count primitive already recorded (R23-01)

chapter_summary: Chapter 23 establishes that triangles (ascending, descending, symmetrical, contracting, and expanding) are all the same underlying structure as the wedge/three-push pattern from chapter 18 -- a trading range with at least three pushes in one direction and two in the other -- distinguished from a wedge mainly by being more horizontal than sloped, and argues that once a market is in one, a breakout is imminent ('breakout mode'). Candidates split into the shared triangle primitive and a two-bar 'oo' miniature-expanding-triangle pattern, a height-based measured-move exit and its beyond-target trend-continuation signal, a tall-enough-to-fade location filter, a weak with-trend breakout bias (explicitly called insufficient alone by Brooks), a breakout-strength confirmation procedure for uncertain wedges, the chapter's most counterintuitive claim (any down-sloping wedge/channel functions as a bull flag regardless of the apparent larger trend), and two research-grade context claims (expanding triangles alternating reversal/continuation roles, triangles late in a trend becoming the final flag). Only two pages of dense conceptual material plus two annotated figures; most figure-specific commentary is worked examples of the general primitives above and was not separately recorded.
